This course is cross-listed under two course numbers. It is all the same class: everyone meets
together Fridays 8:00 to 11:50 AM in 1244 TNRB, works on the same client teams, uses this site,
and uses Canvas as the LMS. Register under whichever number fits your program.

| Course | Section | Title | Credit Hours |
|--------|---------|-------|--------------|
| MBA 693R | 011 | Special Topics in Management | 3.0 |
| STRAT 490R | 001 | Topics in Strategic Management | 3.0 |

## Description

The AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy inside the BYU Marriott School of
Business. Most of the time you will be on a delivery team for a paying client. The client is
paying a fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects professional work. Your grade
reflects both the quality of your work and the professionalism with which you do it.

The Foundry builds software. Discovery work comes first, and its purpose is to decide what to
build. Every engagement ends with software the client is running.

As at any consulting firm, client work arrives on the clients' schedule. There will be times when
you are not staffed to a client project. In those periods you work through a set curriculum
instead, beginning with the Claude Developer certification and then your own product.

Participation is a two-semester sequence, fall and winter.

## Purpose

This course develops students who can take a problem from discovery to production software that
an organization uses, and who can manage the client relationship while they do it.

## Learning Outcomes

| # | Learning Outcome | BYU Aims Supported |
|:-:|:-----------------|:-------------------|
| 1 | Take a problem from discovery through a shipped, production system running in an organization's environment | Intellectually Enlarging |
| 2 | Build with Claude across the API, Claude Code, and Model Context Protocol to the standard validated by the Claude Certified Developer credential | Intellectually Enlarging; Lifelong Learning and Service |
| 3 | Own a workstream for a paying client: scope it, report its status without being asked, and defend the decisions behind it | Character Building; Lifelong Learning and Service |
| 4 | Judge whether a piece of work is worth building at all, weighing cost, risk, and the effect on the people it touches | Spiritually Strengthening; Character Building |
| 5 | Give and receive direct feedback, and change observable behavior in response to it | Character Building; Spiritually Strengthening |

## Prerequisites

**Build**, IS 693R / MSB 341, is the prerequisite. It is offered every fall and every winter.

Exceptions are granted for the 2026-2027 school year, since the Foundry is running for the first
time and nobody has had the chance to take it yet. See
[The Builder and the Consultant](06-builder-and-consultant.qmd) for the three pathways through
this year.

## Required Materials

- **Laptop.** Mac or Windows, capable of running VS Code or Cursor and a local development
  environment. 8GB RAM minimum, more is better.
- **Claude access.** You will have a Claude plan for Foundry work, either provided on the
  Foundry's Claude Enterprise account or reimbursed if you hold your own. The specific plan and
  the mechanism are set each term and communicated before it begins.
- **LMS.** Canvas, for milestone submissions, the video reflection, and grades.
- **Other AI tools.** Anything else you want to use is yours to arrange.

All readings and reference material are on this website at no cost.

## What You Will Work On

Foundry work takes three forms. You will be on one of the first two at any given time, and on
the third throughout.

**Funded engagements.** A client pays a fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects
professional delivery. These carry the tightest obligations.

**Unfunded engagements.** Real outside organizations with real stakes and no fee: nonprofits,
university units, early-stage ventures, and mission-driven work the Foundry takes because it is
worth doing. The standard of work is identical, and the confidentiality and intellectual property
obligations still apply on the terms set for that engagement.

**Studio projects.** The Foundry cannot seat every builder on an outside engagement at once. When
you are not staffed, you build your own product to the same standard, with real users, and ship
it. See [Studio Projects](09-studio-projects.qmd).

**Alongside all three, the certification track.** Every builder works toward the Claude Certified
Developer, Foundations credential. The preparation is coursework and the deliverables feed
whatever project you are on. See [The Certification Track](08-certification.qmd).

Which form you are on is a matter of staffing and timing rather than merit, and it can change
between terms. How you are assigned is set out in
[How Teams Are Staffed](05-how-teams-are-staffed.qmd).

## Time Commitment

| | |
|---|---|
| **Class commitment** | 10 hours per week, including the Friday studio block |
| **Client commitment** | Typically an additional 10 hours per week when client demand calls for it |

The base 10 hours is the course, and it is what 3.0 credit hours per semester represents. The
surge hours are the extra time client delivery takes when a paying client has a deadline.
Surge is not every week, and it is not open-ended, but it is not optional either when your team
is in it.

Students enroll each semester for a total of 6.0 credit hours across the year.

If a week comes when you cannot deliver your hours, tell your team and the faculty advisor in
advance. Told in advance, your team can plan around the missed hours. Found out late, the missed hours
delay work for the client.

## Studio Time

The Friday 8:00 to 11:50 AM block in 1244 TNRB is your team's standing work session: co-working,
cross-team critique, and client calls. Office hours are Wednesdays 1:30 to 3:30 PM in 587 TNRB
and Fridays 3:00 to 3:30 PM by phone. The last 30 minutes on Wednesday are also by phone.

**Required sessions:**

| Session | When |
|---------|------|
| Kick-off, team formation, client introductions | First studio of fall semester |
| Phase review: discovery | Set per engagement |
| Phase review: build | Set per engagement |
| Phase review: transfer and handoff | Set per engagement |
| End-of-year showcase | Final studio of winter semester |

All other Fridays are optional but strongly encouraged. Teams that skip studio time consistently
underperform.

## Schedule

Engagements start on a rolling basis, so this course has no fixed course-wide calendar. Your
team's phase boundaries and milestone dates are set at kick-off and posted in Canvas. The
certification track runs on a common schedule across the cohort; see
[The Certification Track](08-certification.qmd).

## Grading

### Grade Components (500 points possible)

| Component | Points | Weight | Level |
|-----------|--------|--------|-------|
| Weekly Update Emails | 56 pts | 11% | Individual |
| Milestone Deliverables | 160 pts | 32% | Team |
| Client Evaluation | 64 pts | 13% | Team |
| Developmentship | 180 pts | 36% | Individual |
| Video Reflection | 40 pts | 8% | Individual |
| **Base Total** | **500 pts** | 100% | |
| Extra Credit (BYU Student Ratings) | 10 pts | +2% | |

Two components grade the **product and the pod**: milestones and the evaluation of the team, 224
points between them. Three grade **you**: your updates, your developmentship composite, and your
reflection, 276 points. A pod's strong results cannot earn an A for a member who contributed little,
and a strong individual on a struggling pod keeps the 276 individual points they earn.

### Weekly Update Emails (56 points)

Every Saturday you send an individual end-of-week update to **aifoundry@byu.edu**, CC your client
lead: what you accomplished, what you are doing next week, and anything blocking you. 28 emails
across two semesters, 2 points each.

| Status | Points |
|--------|--------|
| On time (Saturday by 11:59 PM) | 2 pts |
| Late (by Monday 8:00 AM) | 1 pt |
| After Monday 8:00 AM | 0 pts |

This component scores **compliance only**: whether the update arrived, on time. Whether it was
any good is graded on the Communication axis of your developmentship composite, from the same
emails, by the people who had to read them. Format, examples, and the distinction from the team's
client update are in [Weekly Updates](03-weekly-updates.qmd).

### Milestone Deliverables (160 points)

Four milestones, 40 points each, graded by the faculty advisor against the
[Build Standards](04-build-standards.qmd), not by the client.

| Milestone | What is due |
|-----------|-------------|
| **D: Discovery** | An AI-specific audit of the organization. Where AI actually helps, what is worth building, what is worth automating, with an estimate and a sequence |
| **B1: Working build** | Software that runs, integrated with real systems or a realistic stand-in, with the architecture documented |
| **B2: Shipped** | Production code running in the client's environment. Tested, deployed, monitored |
| **T: Transfer** | Handoff documentation, a walkthrough with their own people, and a repository they can run without us |

Each milestone is scored on four dimensions, 10 points each: **Correctness**, **Usefulness**,
**Explainability**, and **Craft**. The full rubric is in
[Build Standards](04-build-standards.qmd).

Due dates are set per engagement at kick-off and posted in Canvas. Teams on a discovery-only
engagement complete D and a scaled transfer. Studio projects run the same four milestones, scaled
to one or two builders.

### Client Evaluation (64 points)

Your client evaluates the **team** twice: at mid-term for development only, and at the end of the
year as an input to your grade. Five dimensions, 1 to 5, each with written behavioral
descriptions the client rates against.

| Dimension | The question the client answers |
|-----------|----------------------------------|
| Timeliness | Did the team deliver what they promised, when they promised it? |
| Communication | Could you tell where the work stood without having to ask? |
| Agency | Did the team move the work forward on its own? |
| Technical Competency | Did they build something that actually works? |
| Contribution | Was the output worth the engagement? |

The five dimensions are averaged, and the average converts to points:

| Team average | Points |
|--------------|--------|
| 4.75 to 5.00 | 64 |
| 4.50 to 4.74 | 62 |
| 4.25 to 4.49 | 60 |
| 4.00 to 4.24 | 58 |
| 3.75 to 3.99 | 55 |
| 3.50 to 3.74 | 53 |
| 3.25 to 3.49 | 51 |
| 3.00 to 3.24 | 49 |
| 2.75 to 2.99 | 47 |
| 2.50 to 2.74 | 45 |
| 2.00 to 2.49 | 40 |
| Below 2.00 | Reviewed individually |

**This score is the same for everyone on the pod.** The client also answers a short set of
questions about each of you individually, and those feed your developmentship composite rather
than this component.

On a studio project, your users answer the same five questions in place of a client.

### Developmentship (180 points)

The individual instrument, and the largest single component of your grade. It scores the four
Consultant axes: Judgment, Ownership, Communication, and Collaboration, rated by peers,
clients, and faculty against written behavioral anchors.

The anchors, the three surveys, the weighting, the conversion table, the grade caps, and the
timeline are all set out in [The Developmentship Model](10-developmentship.qmd). Read it in week
1. Nothing in it is a surprise later.

### Video Reflection (40 points)

Every other component measures your work. The video reflection asks what you did with those
measurements.

**Due:** one week after end-of-year feedback is released.
**Submission:** record 2 to 4 minutes. Upload to YouTube (unlisted) or Loom and submit the link
via Canvas.

Before you record, re-read three things: your own self-assessment from before the round, your
development summary, and your calibration gap.

**Prompt.** Four questions.

1. **Your prediction.** Before the round you named the axis you expected to rate highest, the one
   you expected to rate lowest, and the criticism you expected to see. Were you right? Where were
   you off, and why?
2. **The hardest piece of feedback.** Quote one specific thing a reviewer or your client said. Do
   you agree with it? What are you doing about it?
3. **The gap.** Your composite and your self-rating differ. Account for the difference. If they
   matched closely, say what you got right about reading yourself.
4. **Next time.** If you restarted this engagement knowing what you know now, what would you do
   differently?

Keep it conversational. I am looking for honest self-assessment, not polish. A reflection that
admits a mistake and says what changes is worth more than one that explains why every criticism was
situational.

| Criteria | Excellent (10) | Good (7) | Adequate (4) | Weak (0-2) |
|----------|----------------|----------|--------------|------------|
| **Calibration** | Engages the gap between prediction and result directly, and explains it | Notices the gap, explains it thinly | Mentions the gap in passing | Ignores it, or disputes the data instead of engaging it |
| **Engages feedback** | Quotes specific client and peer comments and responds to them | Acknowledges feedback generally | Mentions feedback in passing | Ignores or dismisses |
| **Growth mindset** | Concrete plan tied to a named axis | General intentions | Minimal forward-looking | No reflection on change |
| **Clarity** | Organized, right length, professional | Minor issues | Rambling or too brief | Unprepared or inappropriate |

::: {.callout-note}
Disagreeing with your feedback is allowed and is sometimes correct. What is graded is whether you
engage the evidence behind it. "Three people independently said this and I think they are reading
one incident wrong, here is why" is a strong answer. "I disagree" is not.
:::

### Extra Credit (10 points)

Complete the BYU end-of-semester student ratings survey to earn 10 extra credit points.

### Late Work Policy

Milestone deliverables and the video reflection are accepted up to 9 days late with a 10% penalty
per day.

| Days Late | Penalty |
|-----------|---------|
| 1-3 | -10% to -30% |
| 4-6 | -40% to -60% |
| 7-9 | -70% to -90% |
| 10+ | No credit |

Weekly update emails run on their own schedule, above.

A milestone that is going to slip must be raised with the faculty advisor and the client
**before** the due date, not after. A slip that is flagged early and rescheduled with the client
is a scheduling decision. A slip discovered on the due date is a broken commitment, and it is
graded as one.

## Classroom Culture

**Laptops are the tool.** This is a build studio, so laptops are open and expected. The
obligation that comes with that is attention: if you are in a client call or a critique, you are
in it.

**Cold calling.** I call on people, because when only the most confident students speak, the
class learns less. If you are not ready, say so plainly and I
will come back to you.

**Attendance.** The Friday block is where cross-team critique happens and where most client calls
are scheduled. When you miss it, your teammates cover for you, so treat it as a professional commitment
rather than a class.

## Getting Help

In roughly this order:

- Ask Claude and search this site
- Ask your pod. Someone has probably solved the same problem already
- Bring it to studio time. Do not wait a week with a blocker
- Email or Teams the TAs
- Email or Teams Professor Murff, or come to office hours

Raise blockers within 48 hours. Not at the weekly call, and not at the milestone review.

## Confidentiality and Client Data

Foundry clients share confidential business information: financials, pipelines, customer data,
and strategy. This is a condition of the work, and it carries obligations.

- You will sign the client's NDA, or the Foundry's standard mutual NDA, before receiving data.
- Client data stays in the approved project repository and approved tools. It does not go into
  personal accounts, personal cloud storage, or unapproved AI services.
- Nothing about the project goes on LinkedIn, in a portfolio, or in a job interview without
  written client permission. Ask the faculty advisor first, every time.
- Deliverables and intellectual property belong to the client, not to you and not to BYU.
- When the project ends, you delete local copies of client data.

A confidentiality breach is an Honor Code matter and will also end the engagement. Treat this as
the professional obligation it is.

## AI Use Policy

You are expected to use AI tools extensively. That is the point of the Foundry. The obligations
that come with it:

- **You own the output.** "The model produced it" is not a defense for a wrong number, a
  fabricated citation, or an analysis you cannot explain.
- **Every deliverable must be explainable.** If you cannot walk the client through why the model
  recommends what it recommends, it is not done.
- **Client data goes only into approved tools.** See the confidentiality section above.
- **Disclose your method.** Milestone documentation should say what tools and models you
  used and how you validated the output.

## Instructor Bio

Scott Murff is an Associate Teaching Professor of Strategy at the BYU Marriott School of
Business, where he also serves as faculty advisor and teaches courses on business strategy,
decision-making, and artificial intelligence. He brings over 15 years of experience in
business and technology, having worked as a consultant, product manager, and
data scientist.

Prior to joining BYU, Scott spent nearly seven years at McKinsey & Company in roles ranging
from analytics specialist consultant to principal product manager, where he led product
development and performance management initiatives for Fortune 500 clients. His earlier career
includes building forecasting models as a VP at Zions Bancorporation and conducting regulatory
research at the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Scott holds a Master's degree in Management Science & Engineering from Stanford University and
a B.A. in Economics with a minor in Math, from BYU. He is passionate about helping students
apply AI, analytics, and strategy to meaningful real-world problems with both rigor and purpose.

## Mission and Aims

The mission of Brigham Young University, founded, supported, and guided by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, is to assist individuals in their quest for perfection and eternal life. That assistance should provide a period of intensive learning in a stimulating setting where a commitment to excellence is expected and the full realization of human potential is pursued.

BYU seeks to develop students of faith, intellect, and character who have the skills and the desire to continue learning and to serve others throughout their lives.

A BYU education should be (1) spiritually strengthening, (2) intellectually enlarging, and (3) character building, leading to (4) lifelong learning and service.

Building on the foundational Mission and Aims, the Marriott School of Business aspires to transform the world through Christlike leadership by developing leaders of faith, intellect, and character guided by the following 4 values:

-   **Faith in Christ** - We value deep and abiding faith in Jesus Christ. Our faith gives us the capacity to envision a better future, the confidence to make that future happen, and the courage to act in the face of challenges.

-   **Integrity in Action** - We value integrity and hold ourselves to the highest moral and ethical standards. Acting with integrity builds trust, strengthens character, and focuses our ambitions on things of eternal consequence.

-   **Respect for All** - We value respect for all individuals as children of God and recognize the inherent worth, divine potential, and agency of each person. A climate of respect and belonging enhances our learning, facilitates collaboration, and encourages personal growth.

-   **Excellence** - We value excellence in learning, teaching, research, management, and leadership. An expectation of excellence magnifies our influence and motivates us to continually improve.

We evaluate our decisions and actions by the impact they will have on the academic experience, professional preparation, character development, emotional well-being, and spiritual growth of our students.

## Honor Code

In keeping with the principles of the BYU Honor Code, students are expected to be honest in all of their academic work. Academic honesty means, most fundamentally, that any work you present as your own must in fact be your own work and not that of another. Violations of this principle may result in a failing grade in the course and additional disciplinary action by the university. Students are also expected to adhere to the Dress and Grooming Standards. Adherence demonstrates respect for yourself and others and ensures an effective learning and working environment. It is the university's expectation, and every instructor's expectation in class, that each student will abide by all Honor Code standards. Please call the Honor Code Office at 422-2847 if you have questions about those standards.

## Preventing & Responding to Sexual Misconduct

The health and well-being of students is of paramount importance at Brigham Young University. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment (including sexual violence), there are many resources available for assistance.

In accordance with Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, BYU prohibits unlawful sex discrimination, including sexual harassment, against any participant in its education programs or activities. The university also prohibits sexual harassment by its personnel and students. Sexual harassment occurs when

a person is subjected to unwelcome sexual speech or conduct so severe, pervasive, and offensive that it effectively denies their ability to access any BYU education program or activity; any aid, benefit, or service of BYU is conditioned on a person's participation in unwelcome sexual conduct; or a person suffers sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking on the basis of sex. University policy requires all faculty members to promptly report incidents of sexual harassment that come to their attention in any way, including through face-to-face conversations, a written class assignment or paper, class discussion, email, text, or social media post. Incidents of sexual harassment should be reported to the Title IX Coordinator at t9coordinator@byu.edu or (801) 422-8692 or 1085 WSC. Reports may also be submitted online at https://titleix.byu.edu/report or 1-888-238-1062 (24-hours a day).

BYU offers confidential resources for those affected by sexual harassment, including the university's Sexual Assault Survivor Advocate, as well as a number of non-confidential resources and services that may be helpful. Additional information about Title IX, the university's Sexual Harassment Policy, reporting requirements, and resources can be found at http://titleix.byu.edu or by contacting the university's Title IX Coordinator.

## Student Disability

Brigham Young University is committed to providing a working and learning atmosphere that reasonably accommodates qualified persons with disabilities. A disability is a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities. Whether an impairment is substantially limiting depends on its nature and severity, its duration or expected duration, and its permanent or expected permanent or long-term impact. Examples include vision or hearing impairments, physical disabilities, chronic illnesses, emotional disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), learning disorders, and attention disorders (e.g., ADHD). If you have a disability which impairs your ability to complete this course successfully, please contact the University Accessibility Center (UAC), 2170 WSC or 801-422-2767 to request a reasonable accommodation. The UAC can also assess students for learning, attention, and emotional concerns. If you feel you have been unlawfully discriminated against on the basis of disability, please contact the Equal Opportunity Office at 801-422-5895, eo_manager@byu.edu, or visit https://hrs.byu.edu/equal-opportunity for help.
